prose.summary: A sommelier runs the wine program for a restaurant or hotel: building the list, pricing it, training the floor staff to sell it, and standing at the table to talk a stranger into (or out of) the bottle they were about to order. People confuse it with being a wine buyer, but a buyer's job ends at the invoice; a sommelier's job is the service itself, the read on the guest, the timing of the pour. The postings behind this title lean hospitality-operations as much as palate: scheduling, budgeting, and POS systems show up almost as often as anything about wine.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split between the cellar and the floor: counting bottles against the POS report, chasing a distributor about a delayed allocation, and rewriting a page of the list because a vintage sold out faster than expected. There's usually one big service push (Friday and Saturday night, or a private event) where you're on your feet for six hours straight, tasting nothing but pouring constantly. Mornings tend to be paperwork: invoices, temperature logs on the storage room, a staff pre-shift where you walk the servers through what's new by the glass. The moment people in this job wait for is the pairing that lands, when a guest who ordered the wrong wine for their dish takes your suggestion instead and comes back a month later asking for you by name. Budgeting and cost percentages eat more of the week than most outsiders assume; tasting is maybe an hour of it, if that. The rest is inventory, training, and making sure the list still makes sense against what's selling.
prose.work_environment: This is a floor job, not a desk job: you're standing in a dining room or a cellar for most of a shift, and the remote share on this role sits at zero because the work is physically tied to a specific building's inventory and a specific room full of guests. Hours run nights and weekends by default, since that's when people drink wine with dinner, and the worst weeks are around holidays (Valentine's, New Year's, big private events) when the list has to be right and the staff has to be drilled on it beforehand. Storage rooms are cold by design, service floors are warm and loud, and you move between both several times a night. There's real physical wear in this (a lot of walking, a lot of standing, some heavy case-lifting) that people don't picture when they imagine the job as sipping and swirling.
prose.getting_in: There's no license gate here, but there is an experience one: postings that state a figure put the median at 5 years, and the credentialing bodies (WSET, Court of Master Sommeliers) that most employers recognize run their own multi-year tracks alongside that floor experience. The realistic path is to get hired into a wine-adjacent floor job first (server, back-of-house at a wine-focused restaurant) and study for certifications while working service, rather than trying to certify first and get hired second. The longest stretch is usually years three through five, when you know the material but need enough service reps to run a room solo under pressure. The common stall point is money: entry-level floor jobs pay modestly while the certification exams and required tastings are paid out of pocket. Formal education barely shows up as a requirement in these postings; what employers are screening for is food-and-beverage experience (a third of postings name it directly) and comfort with catering and operations, not a degree.
prose.ladder: Early on you're pouring and answering questions; the first real step up is owning the list itself, meaning you pick what's on it, negotiate with distributors, and answer for the margin on it. From there the ladder forks: some sommeliers move into beverage director roles across multiple properties (more budgeting, more SAP or accounting work, less time on the floor), and others stay hands-on at one restaurant and go deep on rarity and allocation instead of scale. That fork usually happens somewhere in years five to eight. Management-track sommeliers pick up hiring, payroll, and HR operations work that has nothing to do with wine; floor-track ones trade that for more direct guest contact and more say over what's poured.
prose.suits: People who come alive in this job are the ones who like reading a stranger in ten seconds flat: what they're nervous about, what they want to spend, what they'll be embarrassed to admit they don't know. The good day is the six-top where nobody agreed on red or white until you found the one bottle that worked for all of them. People who leave tend to be the ones who wanted this to be mostly about the wine itself: the tasting, the terroir, the study. They find out the job is scheduling and inventory and a Friday night on your feet, and they go looking for something closer to the vineyard side (importing, distribution) where the wine knowledge is the whole job instead of half of it.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly tasting and talking about wine; the postings say otherwise; budgeting, accounting, and operations skills show up as often or more often than anything tasting-related. Another one: people think a deep palate is the hard part to acquire, when the harder skill is reading a table fast enough to sell confidently without sounding like you're upselling.
prose.who_qualifies: The strongest routes in are Hotel Manager and Chef, and that's not a coincidence: both jobs already require running a floor or a kitchen under pressure, managing a schedule, and handling a budget, which is most of what a sommelier does when they're not pouring. What doesn't carry over automatically is the wine knowledge itself; a chef or hotel manager moving into this role still has to put in the study and tasting hours a dedicated wine background gives you for free.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what it feels like to be wrong in front of a table, recommending a bottle that doesn't land and having to recover the moment gracefully while the guest watches you do it. It also can't capture the physical toll of a six-hour Saturday service on your feet, which is a real part of why people leave that no salary figure explains.

steps.do: Get hired onto a wine-focused floor
steps.how: Start as a server or back-of-house staff at a restaurant with an actual wine program, not just a bar. This takes a few weeks of job hunting and is the foundation everything else builds on; you know you're in the right spot when the restaurant has someone senior you can shadow.

These are the entry-level wine certifications most sommelier job postings recognize, run over a few weeks to a couple of months depending on the provider. You're done with this step when you can pass the exam and explain, unprompted, why two wines from the same grape taste different from different regions.

steps.do: Work service for two to three years
steps.how: This is where you build the floor instincts no course teaches: reading a table, upselling without sounding like it, recovering when a recommendation misses. There's no shortcut on the clock here; it's the years, not the study, that make the difference.

steps.do: Pursue Court of Master Sommeliers certification
steps.how: The Certified and Advanced levels take structured study alongside full-time service work, often another year or two beyond WSET. This is the step that separates a floor sommelier from someone who can eventually run a program; you know you're ready to sit for it when you can blind-taste a wine and correctly guess its region under time pressure.

steps.do: Take ownership of a wine list
steps.how: Move into a role (or push for one at your current restaurant) where you pick the list, negotiate with distributors, and answer for the food and beverage cost percentage. This usually lands around the five-year mark and is the point where you're a sommelier running a program, not just working a floor.

prose.tools: Toast POS shows up directly in these postings and is the real gatekeeper: if you can't run inventory and sales reports through a POS system, you can't do the budgeting half of this job. Accounting and SAP knowledge appear in a meaningful share of postings too, mostly at properties large enough to need formal cost reporting. The wine-specific tools (cellar management software, allocation trackers) barely register in postings compared to general restaurant operations software, which tells you where hiring managers are looking when they screen a resume.

industries.name: Independent fine-dining restaurants
industries.note: Smallest team, most direct control over the list, but the budget and the ceiling are both lower than a hotel program.

industries.name: Hotels and resorts
industries.note: Larger wine programs, more structured career path (routes in from Hotel Manager reflect this), but more layers of approval before a bottle makes the list.

industries.name: Catering and events companies
industries.note: Catering shows up in a quarter of these postings; the work is less about one room's regulars and more about pricing and pouring for one-off crowds you'll never see again.

industries.name: Private clubs
industries.note: Smaller, more consistent guest base you get to know by name, but a more conservative, less experimental list than a restaurant chasing reviews.

specializations.name: Beverage director (multi-property)
specializations.why: Takes the budgeting and operations side of the job further, overseeing programs across several restaurants or hotel properties instead of one room; this is where accounting and SAP skills stop being optional.

specializations.name: Rare and allocated wine buying
specializations.why: For sommeliers who stay hands-on rather than go into management, deep relationships with distributors for limited-allocation bottles become the differentiator that lets a small independent restaurant compete with a hotel's buying power.

specializations.name: Beverage program consulting
specializations.why: Experienced sommeliers who've built one strong list often get pulled into building others for new restaurant openings, working project to project instead of holding one floor job.

pros: The pairing that lands is an immediate, visible win: you watch a guest's reaction change mid-sip, which is a kind of feedback most jobs never give you in real time.
The knowledge compounds in a way that's genuinely interesting for years, not months; there's always another region, another vintage, another producer you haven't tasted yet.
A part-time option exists at a real share of these postings, which is unusual in hospitality and makes this workable alongside other commitments in a way a full kitchen role often isn't.
The skill set (reading people, managing a budget, running a small operation) transfers cleanly into hotel management or chef roles if you want to move sideways later.
cons: The pay ceiling is modest for the years of study required; the top quarter of these postings tops out well below what the certification investment might suggest.
Nights, weekends, and holidays are the job, not an exception to it, and that doesn't change as you get more senior.
A meaningful chunk of the work (invoices, scheduling, cost percentages) has nothing to do with wine and can't be avoided even at senior levels.
The physical toll of standing through six-hour services adds up over a career in a way that's easy to underestimate at 25.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a sommelier
faq.a: Figure on roughly five years from entry-level floor job to running your own list, based on the median experience level in current postings. Certification exams (WSET, Court of Master Sommeliers) run alongside that service work rather than before it, so the years overlap rather than stack.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a sommelier
faq.a: No: education requirements barely appear in these postings at all. What employers screen for is food-and-beverage experience and floor-service history, and the wine certifications (WSET, Court of Master Sommeliers) function as the credential a degree would in other fields.

faq.q: is being a sommelier a good career right now
faq.a: It depends heavily on what you want from it: the work itself stays interesting for years and the skills transfer into hotel or restaurant management, but the pay ceiling shown in current postings is modest for the study investment required. It suits people who'd do the wine study anyway, for its own sake, not just for the paycheck.

No, and the postings back this up directly: the remote share for this role sits at zero. The job is tied to a specific cellar's inventory and a specific dining room's guests, which is not work you can do from a laptop.

faq.q: sommelier vs wine buyer, what's the difference
faq.a: A wine buyer's job largely ends once the bottle is purchased and priced; a sommelier's job is the service itself, standing at the table and matching a specific bottle to a specific guest in the moment. Many sommeliers do buying as part of their role once they're running a list, but the floor work is what defines the title.
